title: Policy Gradient Methods
summary: Learning a policy directly instead of deriving it from value estimates, up through PPO — the industry-standard algorithm behind RLHF.

slides.markdown:
Value-based methods (see [value-based-methods](value-based-methods)) derive a policy indirectly — "take the action with the highest Q-value." That works cleanly for a handful of discrete actions, but breaks down for **continuous action spaces** (steering angle, joint torque, portfolio weight) where you can't enumerate every action to take an `argmax`.

**Policy gradient methods** sidestep this by learning a policy `π(a|s;θ)` directly — a parameterized function that outputs an action (or a distribution over actions) given a state, trained to maximize expected return. No value lookup or `argmax` required at decision time.

The core mechanic: nudge the probability of an action **up** if it led to good outcomes, and **down** if it led to bad ones. Formally, the policy gradient theorem says the gradient of expected return with respect to policy parameters is proportional to `∇log π(a|s) · G` — the direction that increases the log-probability of the action taken, scaled by how good the resulting return `G` turned out to be.

Intuitively: if an action led to a big positive return, reinforce it strongly; if it led to a poor return, suppress it. Repeated over many episodes, actions that reliably lead to good outcomes become more likely.

**REINFORCE** is the most basic policy gradient algorithm: run a full episode, compute the actual observed return `G` at each step, and update the policy using that return as the scaling factor for every action taken along the way.

It's simple and unbiased, but has a serious practical flaw: because it uses the raw, full-episode return as the signal, and that return can vary wildly between runs of the same policy just from environment randomness, the gradient estimates are **extremely high-variance** — training is noisy and sample-inefficient.

**Actor-critic** methods fix REINFORCE's variance problem by adding a learned **critic** — a value function that estimates a baseline expected return for a state. Instead of scaling the policy update by the raw return `G`, you scale it by the **advantage** `A = G − V(s)`: how much better the actual outcome was than what was expected anyway.

The **actor** is the policy being trained; the **critic** is the value function providing the baseline. Subtracting a baseline doesn't change the expected gradient (it's mathematically unbiased) but dramatically reduces its variance — the update only reacts to *surprising* outcomes, not to noise that would have happened regardless of the action taken.

**PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization)** is the industry-standard policy gradient algorithm today. The problem it solves: a naive policy update can be too large, moving the policy so far in one step that it collapses performance and never recovers (unlike supervised learning, a bad policy update also corrupts the *data you collect next*, compounding the damage).

PPO's fix is a **clipped objective** — it caps how much the probability ratio between the new and old policy is allowed to change in a single update, preventing any one step from moving the policy too far from what it just was. This gives most of the stability of more complex trust-region methods with far simpler implementation, which is why it became the default choice in practice, including for RLHF (see [rlhf-alignment](rlhf-alignment)).

| | Value-based (Q-learning/DQN) | Policy-based (REINFORCE/PPO) |
|---|---|---|
| Action space | Discrete (needs argmax) | Discrete or continuous |
| What's learned | A value function; policy is implicit | A policy directly |
| Stability | Can be unstable (deadly triad) | Naive versions high-variance; PPO addresses this |
| Output | A single best action | Can naturally output a stochastic policy |

**How to decide:** reach for policy gradients whenever the action space is continuous or you specifically want a stochastic policy (useful for exploration or multi-agent settings); value-based methods are simpler and often more sample-efficient when actions are genuinely discrete and few.

slides.sectionTitle: Why PPO is the go-to for RLHF
slides.markdown:
RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) treats a language model as a policy being optimized against a learned reward model. This setting is exactly where PPO's stability guarantees matter most: a language model policy that drifts too far in one update can degrade into incoherent or degenerate text, and there's no way to "undo" a bad update once it's shipped generating training data for the next round.

PPO's clipped updates keep each optimization step close to the previous policy, which is precisely the property needed to fine-tune a pretrained language model without destroying its pretrained capabilities in a single bad step.

slides.sectionTitle: Entropy bonus: keeping the policy from collapsing early
slides.markdown:
Left unchecked, a policy gradient update can push the policy toward near-certainty on whatever action looked best early in training, collapsing exploration before it's found a genuinely good strategy — once the policy is nearly deterministic, it stops generating the varied experience needed to discover better actions.

The standard fix adds an **entropy bonus** to the training objective: a term that rewards the policy for staying spread out over actions, not just for maximizing return. Weighted by a small coefficient, it keeps enough randomness alive during training to keep exploring, and is typically annealed down as training progresses and the policy has more reason to commit to what it's learned works.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: why policy gradient methods are sample-hungry
slides.markdown:
Training a PPO agent to a strong policy on a moderately complex simulated task (a robotic locomotion benchmark, an Atari game) commonly takes tens of millions of environment steps — for Atari, published results often cite 10-40 million frames per game to reach human-level performance. Compare that to a supervised classifier reaching strong accuracy on tens of thousands of labeled examples.

The gap exists because each gradient update only uses on-policy data collected under the *current* policy (old rollouts become stale and unusable the moment the policy changes), unlike supervised learning where a fixed labeled dataset can be reused across the entire training run. This sample cost is the practical reason RL is rarely applied where real-world trial-and-error is expensive or slow to collect.
